candidates.quote: I meant to write about death, only life came breaking in as usual.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.locator: the entry for 17 February 1922 (ed. Leonard Woolf, Hogarth Press, 1953)
candidates.whyThisMonth: An impermanence line that refuses to become an elegy: you sit down to brood on what passes and the morning interrupts you.

candidates.quote: As autumn advances, the Tsuchimikado mansion looks unutterably beautiful.
candidates.author: Murasaki Shikibu
candidates.whyThisMonth: A thousand years ago a woman opened her diary by noticing that the season was going, and that this was exactly why the house looked so beautiful.

candidates.quote: Imitate the trees. Learn to lose in order to recover, and remember that nothing stays the same for long, not even pain, psychic pain.
candidates.author: May Sarton
candidates.locator: the entry for October 6th, p. 34 (W. W. Norton, 1973)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month’s hardest consolation put plainly at the start of a day: whatever is heavy this morning is also a thing that passes.

candidates.quote: God knows I never sought anything in you except yourself; I wanted simply you, nothing of yours.
candidates.author: Heloise
candidates.work: The Letters of Abelard and Heloise
candidates.locator: Letter 2, Heloise’s first letter to Abelard, p. 51 (Penguin Classics, 1974)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Everything around this love was taken away and the sentence is still standing, which is the month’s question about what stays answered by a woman who knows.

candidates.quote: I am certain of nothing but of the holiness of the Heart’s affections and the truth of Imagination.
candidates.author: John Keats
candidates.locator: 22 November 1817 (The Letters of John Keats 1814 to 1821, ed. H. E. Rollins, 1958, vol. 1)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A man of twenty-two names the two things he would keep if everything else went, which is the only useful way to start a day about what does not last.

candidates.quote: No entertainment is so cheap as reading, nor any pleasure so lasting.
candidates.author: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
candidates.work: letter to her daughter, the Countess of Bute
candidates.locator: 30 May 1756 (The Complete Letters, ed. Robert Halsband, 1967, vol. 3, p. 107)
candidates.whyThisMonth: In a month of passing things, a grandmother points at the one pleasure she has found that does not wear out, and it costs nothing.

candidates.quote: It is possible that some word of me may have come to you, though even this is doubtful, since an insignificant and obscure name will scarcely penetrate far in either time or space.
candidates.author: Petrarch
candidates.locator: the opening sentence, Seniles XVIII, 1 (Petrarch: The First Modern Scholar and Man of Letters, trans. Robinson, 1898)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous poet in Europe writes to people not yet born and assumes they have never heard of him, which is a gentle cure for taking this morning’s reputation seriously.

candidates.quote: If we want things to stay as they are, things will have to change.
candidates.author: Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa
candidates.speaker: Tancredi Falconeri
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence that turns the month’s subject into a practical morning instruction: what you want to keep, you will have to let move.

candidates.quote: Whatever we had missed, we possessed together the precious, the incommunicable past.
candidates.author: Willa Cather
candidates.locator: Book V, Cuzak’s Boys, chapter III, the closing sentence
candidates.speaker: Jim Burden
candidates.whyThisMonth: It says the years that went are a possession and not a loss, which is the kindest thing the theme can be made to say at six in the morning.

candidates.quote: Pause you who read this, and think for a moment of the long chain of iron or gold, of thorns or flowers, that would never have bound you, but for the formation of the first link on one memorable day.
candidates.author: Charles Dickens
candidates.speaker: Pip
candidates.whyThisMonth: It asks the reader to stop, on the one day of the year they are holding, and see that an ordinary morning is where a whole life turns out to have begun.

candidates.quote: The flow of the river is ceaseless and its water is never the same.
candidates.author: Kamo no Chōmei
candidates.locator: the opening sentence, in Anthology of Japanese Literature (Grove Press, 1955)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The opening line of the classic essay on impermanence, and it is a river rather than a grave: the theme arrives as something moving, not something ending.

candidates.quote: Time is the substance I am made of. Time is a river which sweeps me along, but I am the river.
candidates.author: Jorge Luis Borges
candidates.work: Other Inquisitions, A New Refutation of Time
candidates.locator: the closing paragraph (University of Texas Press, 1964)
candidates.whyThisMonth: After a whole essay arguing time away, Borges concedes it and turns the concession into company: the reader is not a victim of the passing, they are it.

candidates.quote: I think we are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not.
candidates.author: Joan Didion
candidates.work: Slouching Towards Bethlehem, On Keeping a Notebook
candidates.whyThisMonth: The selves you have already lost are the first impermanence anyone meets, and this gives the reader a manageable morning task: nod to them.

candidates.quote: For nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed; the earth is always shifting, the light is always changing, the sea does not cease to grind down rock.
candidates.author: James Baldwin
candidates.whyThisMonth: Baldwin states the month’s premise as good news: if nothing holds still, then nothing that is wrong this morning is permanent either.

candidates.quote: I had a farm in Africa, at the foot of the Ngong Hills.
candidates.author: Isak Dinesen
candidates.locator: Book One, The Ngong Farm, chapter 1, the opening sentence
candidates.whyThisMonth: Eight words in the past tense, and the whole elegy is already inside them: this is what it sounds like to have had something and to say so calmly.

candidates.quote: In spite of illness, in spite even of the arch-enemy sorrow, one can remain alive long past the usual date of disintegration if one is unafraid of change, insatiable in intellectual curiosity, interested in big things, and happy in small ways.
candidates.author: Edith Wharton
candidates.whyThisMonth: Wharton at seventy-two names being unafraid of change as the thing that keeps a person alive, which is the month’s theme turned into a way to get up.
